hook: He sold Japanese running shoes from his car boot. Then he built Nike.
summary: Phil Knight wrote a Stanford class paper arguing Japanese running shoes could beat German ones, then started importing Onitsuka Tigers and selling them at track meets with his old coach Bill Bowerman. For years the company, Blue Ribbon Sports, lived on the edge: banks cut off credit and the Japanese supplier tried to drop them. Forced to make their own shoe, they launched Nike in 1971 and built the world's biggest sportswear brand.

summary: A Danish carpenter, Ole Kirk Christiansen, started making wooden toys in Billund during the Great Depression and later bet on plastic bricks. By the early 2000s LEGO had over-expanded into theme parks, clothing and too many new parts, and it was losing money fast. New CEO Jørgen Vig Knudstorp cut the complexity, sold what wasn't core and refocused on the brick, starting one of business history's great turnarounds.

Ray Kroc, a struggling salesman of milkshake mixers, saw it and pushed to franchise it across America, later buying the brothers out. The secret of the empire turned out to be real estate as much as burgers, and the story raises hard questions about who deserves credit.

He started again in Bentonville, studied competitors obsessively and opened the first Walmart in 1962, betting that small towns deserved low prices. Discipline on costs and a love of learning made it the world's largest retailer.

hook: Family feuds nearly destroyed Gucci, and ended in a murder.
summary: Guccio Gucci started a leather goods shop in Florence in 1921 after working at a London hotel. His sons and grandsons turned it into a global brand but fought each other bitterly, and Maurizio Gucci was murdered in 1995 on orders from his ex-wife. Outside managers and designers revived Gucci, which is now owned by Kering.

hook: A tyre company invented the world's most famous restaurant stars. Here's why.
summary: Brothers André and Édouard Michelin ran a tyre company in France when there were only a few thousand cars on the roads. In 1900 they published a free guide to help drivers, hoping more driving meant more tyres sold. That guide became the Michelin star system that rules fine dining today.

hook: A college paper said overnight delivery could work. He bet everything on it.
summary: Fred Smith outlined an overnight delivery system in a Yale paper and, after serving in Vietnam, founded Federal Express in 1971. The early years nearly bankrupted it, with fuel bills and payrolls hard to meet. The hub-and-spoke system he built changed global logistics.
